purpose: Six recovered concept studies checked for duplicates and added to the published gallery.

continuity.method: Existing artwork inspected; its visual direction and confirmed design carried into text prompts. No image attached to generation calls.

images.title: Through the service wall
images.prompt: Use case: stylized-concept. Asset type: one finished cinematic concept artwork for the cooperative game In to the Crackrooms. Existing project art establishes a photorealistic, tactile industrial Backrooms world: stale yellow fluorescent lights, worn practical equipment, company-employed researchers in yellow protective workwear, an immense spherical imploded region suspended above a chasm. Keep that continuity, but create a distinct new composition. Landscape 3:2, 1536x1024. Restrained atmospheric realism, strong readable shapes, detailed material surfaces, mundane architecture made unsettling. No typography, captions, logos, watermark or UI. No faces, eyes or mouth on the sphere. This is exploratory art, not a mechanics diagram. View from INSIDE a freshly opened narrow cylindrical bore through the Abandoned Utility Halls layer, looking outward toward a scaffold and a sliver of the curved reflective shell above a vast void. The near walls are compressed concrete, severed copper pipes and dense conduits arranged in curved strata. Two yellow-suited researchers work at the bore mouth: one guides a heavy helical mechanical auger mounted on a braced stand while the other inspects a core sample tray. Camera at pipe height, strong circular frame, warm dust caught in practical work lights and cold distant haze. Functional equipment, supported floor, no laser weapons. Focus on the density and scale of excavating an imploded service infrastructure.
images.alt: Two researchers operate a braced auger and inspect core samples inside a pipe-lined bore overlooking scaffolding and the sphere.
images.caption: A service wall becomes an excavation face. Dense pipes and concrete give the established Utility Halls auger gate a tactile setting; the sample-handling arrangement is a visual proposal.
images.question: What should the exposed cross-section tell the team before they choose where to drill?

No faces, eyes or mouth on the sphere. This is exploratory art, not a mechanics diagram. Low camera at the edge of a shallow turquoise pool inside an exposed Poolrooms stratum. White tiled arches recede in a diagonal rhythm, but one blocked arch and its reflected waterline split into sketch-like offset outlines and missing geometry. A yellow-suited researcher stands on a dry grated platform using a restrained handheld reality tool to make a small part of the obstructing tile fully tangible. A teammate watches the tile boundary. Huge curved excavated rim glimpsed in the far side opening establishes this architecture belongs inside a sphere. Humid diffused light, turquoise and chalk white against workwear yellow; localized faint cyan, no cyberpunk neon. The misaligned reflection is the main unsettling discovery, not a monster.

images.caption: The Poolrooms reality-tool gate meets an unreliable reflection. Split tiles and a displaced waterline explore how unstable geometry could become readable before excavation.
images.question: Which mismatch should players notice first: the tile edge, its reflection, or the waterline?

images.question: Which ordinary landmark would help players recognize a repeated passage instead of simply feeling lost?

Two yellow-gloved hands: one applies solvent from a small utilitarian applicator precisely along an adhesive seam, the other lifts a broad curling strip of faded yellow patterned wallpaper. images.caption: A close study of the established Threshold solvent gate. Paper fibers, softened film and the first hint of tissue explore feedback for peeling away the final covering.
images.question: What change in the adhesive should signal that the wallpaper is ready to peel?
